To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the exhalation airflow can be represented by sinusoidal functions of the time for breathing and a time-independent function for talking, and the area of the mouth/nose openings can be regarded as a time-independent constant.
the exhaled airflow rate over time can represented as sinusoidal functions for breathing and a constants for talking.

the exhaled airflow from the breathing and the talking processes can be modeled as sinusoidal and constant functions, respectively, and the direction of the airflow and the area of the mouth/nose openings can be regarded as constant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing models for the flow rate and direction, and area opening of the mouth and nose.
the development of models that can predict the exhaled air flow rate and flow direction for breathing and talking.
the thermo fluid characteristics and the source model for exhalation during breathing and the talking processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the exhalation flow rate over time during breathing and talking can be represented as sinusoidal and constant functions, respectively.

the exhaled airflow from the mouth/nose of the human subject can be characterized by the source model developed in the present study and the model can be useful for predicting the infectious virus transmission.

the exhalation flow rate over time during breathing and talking can be described by sinusoidal and constant functions, respectively, the flow direction did not vary among the subjects, the area of mouth opening was not correlated with the subject's physiological parameters, and the mouth opening area could be regarded as constant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the flow rate of exhalation can be represented by a sinusoidal function and a constant for breathing and talking respectively.
the flow rate and flow direction can be represented as sinusoidal functions and constant, respectively for the breathing process.
the exhaled airflow from the mouth/nose of human subjects could be modeled by a source model that is based on the physiological parameters of a human.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the exhalation flow rate and direction can be represented as sinusoidal and constant functions respectively.
the flow boundary conditions can be described by a set of equations that are functions of physiological parameters of the subject.
the flow rate over time during exhalation can be represented as sinusoidal function for the breathing and a constant function for talking.
